title: Stability and Phase Margin
intro: A feedback system is stable if its closed-loop poles are in the left half plane. The Bode plot of the loop gain shows how close it is to the edge (Razavi, Sections 10.1 to 10.3).

blocks.text: Barkhausen's conditions
Write the closed loop as $Y/X = H/(1 + \beta H)$. At a frequency where

the gain is infinite and the circuit amplifies its own noise into an oscillation at $\omega_1$. These conditions involve only the loop transmission, not where the input and output are. The negative-feedback subtraction already gives $180^{\circ}$; the loop's own $180^{\circ}$ makes $360^{\circ}$, so the returning signal reinforces the original, and a loop gain of at least one lets it grow. Either view is useful: too much gain at the frequency where the phase hits $-180^{\circ}$, or too much phase at the frequency where the gain falls to one.

Two frequencies matter: the gain crossover (GX), where $|\beta H| = 1$, and the phase crossover (PX), where $\angle\beta H = -180^{\circ}$. A stable design has GX well below PX. For $\beta = 1$, GX equals the op amp's unity-gain bandwidth.
Bode-plot reminders

items: Each pole bends the magnitude by $-20$ dB/dec, each zero by $+20$ dB/dec.
A pole's phase starts falling about a decade below it, is $-45^{\circ}$ at the pole and nears $-90^{\circ}$ a decade above. A zero does the opposite in the left half plane.
So poles and zeros affect phase at much lower frequencies than they affect magnitude: an extra high-frequency pole moves PX much more than GX.
Do not confuse the loop-gain plot with the closed-loop response: if GX and PX coincide, the closed loop has infinite gain there even though $|\beta H|$ looks ordinary.

blocks.text: Poles in the s-plane

A closed-loop pole $s_p = \sigma_p + j\omega_p$ contributes a term $e^{(\sigma_p + j\omega_p)t}$ to the impulse response. With $\sigma_p > 0$ (right half plane) it grows; on the $j\omega$ axis it oscillates steadily; in the left half plane it decays. Plotting how the poles move as the loop gain rises is the root locus.
One, two and three poles

One pole, $H = A_0/(1 + s/\omega_0)$: the phase never exceeds $-90^{\circ}$, so the loop is stable for any $\beta \ge 0$. The closed-loop pole is real at $-\omega_0(1 + \beta A_0)$ and moves left as the loop gain grows.
Two poles: the phase approaches but never reaches $-180^{\circ}$, so the loop is stable, though its phase margin can be small. The closed-loop poles solve

They start at $-\omega_{p1}$ and $-\omega_{p2}$, move toward each other, meet when $(\omega_{p1} + \omega_{p2})^2 = 4(1 + \beta A_0)\omega_{p1}\omega_{p2}$, then split vertically into a complex pair with constant real part $-(\omega_{p1} + \omega_{p2})/2$. They never cross into the right half plane, but they become very underdamped.

Three poles: the third pole's phase pulls PX down to a finite frequency, below which GX may now lie or not. Weaker feedback (smaller $\beta$) moves GX down while PX stays, so amplifiers built for higher closed-loop gain are more stable.
Phase margin
How the closed loop behaves at GX follows directly: $Y/X = (1/\beta)\,\beta H/(1 + \beta H)$ with $|\beta H| = 1$ and phase $-180^{\circ} + PM$:

items: PM = 5°: $|1 + \beta H| = 0.087$, an 11-fold peak; the step response rings for a long time.
PM = 45° (GX at the second pole of a two-pole loop): $|1 + \beta H| = 0.765$, a 30% peak at GX.
PM = 60°: $|1 + \beta H| = 1$, so the closed-loop gain at GX is exactly $1/\beta$; little ringing and fast settling. This is the usual target.
Larger PM: more stable, but the response is overdamped and slower.

blocks.alt: Two panels. Left: closed-loop magnitude against normalized frequency for phase margins of 30, 45, 60 and 75 degrees; lower margins show higher peaks near the crossover. Right: the corresponding step responses; 30 degrees overshoots about 40 percent and rings, 45 about 23 percent, 60 under 10 percent, and 75 rises without overshoot.
blocks.caption: A two-pole loop (dominant pole near the origin) closed with unity feedback, for several phase margins.

blocks.text: In a two-pole loop with the first pole far below GX, the margin is set by the second pole: $PM = 90^{\circ} - \tan^{-1}(\omega_u/\omega_{p2})$. GX at the second pole gives 45°; for any useful margin the unity-gain bandwidth must stay below the op amp's second pole.

widget.title: Step response of a feedback amplifier with two poles

blocks.text: The slider sets the second pole relative to the loop's unity-gain frequency. At 1 the margin is 45° with substantial overshoot; at 2 it is 63° and well damped; at 0.5 it is 27° and rings badly.

Phase margin is a small-signal concept. A large step makes the op amp slew and moves its bias points, shifting poles and zeros during the transient, so large-signal settling can ring even with 65° of small-signal margin. Check large-signal behaviour with transient simulations.

blocks.title: Phase margin of a two-pole loop
blocks.text: A loop has a dominant pole and a second pole at twice the unity-gain frequency. Find the phase margin.
solution: The first pole gives $-90^{\circ}$ at crossover. The second gives $-\tan^{-1}(0.5) = -26.6^{\circ}$.

blocks.title: Peaking at 45°
blocks.text: For a loop with 45° phase margin, by how much does the closed-loop gain at the gain crossover exceed $1/\beta$?
solution: $\beta H = e^{-j135^{\circ}}$, so $1 + \beta H = 1 - 0.707 - j0.707$, with magnitude 0.765.

blocks.title: When do the poles go complex?
blocks.text: A two-pole loop has $\omega_{p1} = 1$ Mrad/s and $\omega_{p2} = 100$ Mrad/s. Above what loop gain $\beta A_0$ do the closed-loop poles become complex?

blocks.title: Weaker feedback
blocks.text: An op amp is compensated for 60° margin as a unity-gain buffer (dominant pole effectively at the origin, second pole at $1.73\,\omega_u$). What is the margin with $\beta = 0.5$?
solution: Halving $\beta$ lowers $|\beta H|$ by 6 dB; on a $-20$ dB/dec slope GX moves to $\omega_u/2$.
